schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch deny the title is a motto of the contents — it bears on the music, and nechiloth, if from nachal, may mean 'swarms' of bees, a melody; Ellicott glosses 'meditation' as a word cognate with 'meditate' in Ps. 1:2, a whispered muttering.

Clarke derives nechiloth from a root 'to bore through' (wind-instruments) but records the LXX 'her who obtains the inheritance' (from nachal); Wesley reads 'meditation' as prayer with deep thoughts and fervent affections.

Henry calls Nehiloth 'a word nowhere else used,' conjecturing wind-instruments; Spurgeon distinguishes two sorts of prayer — words and unuttered longings — 'words are not the essence but the garments of prayer.'

Gill reads 'give ear to my words' of vocal prayer (the boldness/parrhesia of the saints), set against the silent meditation of the heart; Calvin declines to solve the title's riddle and hears in the 'meditation' dove-like mournings and sighing.
Augustine hears the whole psalm as the voice of the Church, called to her inheritance that she may herself become the inheritance of the Lord.

sides.position: wind-instruments (flutes, from a root 'to be hollow, to bore through')
a musical tune or melody, perhaps 'swarms' of bees (a hummed air)
'inheritances' (from nachal, to inherit) — read of the Church that inherits through Christ

outliers.note: Reads the whole psalm allegorically as the voice of the Church called to her inheritance, that she may herself become the inheritance of the Lord.

schools.summary: Henry makes 'my King and my God' the most commanding principle and prevailing plea of prayer — kings must yet be beggars at God's throne; Spurgeon calls the little pronouns 'the pith and marrow of the plea,' ours by covenant, promise, oath, and blood.
Gill hears in 'the voice of my cry' a loud outcry of a soul in distress, and the first argument — David's own interest in and relation to the Lord.

Keil and Delitzsch note the grammar — the adjective for 'having pleasure' takes the accusative, the verb 'to sojourn' governs its object directly — so that evil, as a person, cannot lodge with a holy God.
Clarke traces the waking soul's process to importunate prayer, and preserves Jarchi's turn: when able, 'give ear to my words'; when fear seizes the heart, 'consider my meditation.'

Clarke reads a morning hymn answering the evening hymn, and the archer's image in 'direct my prayer' — aim, shoot, and look up; Wesley: 'every morning; as soon as I wake … the first thing I do is pray to thee.'

Ellicott renders 'direct' as 'prepare' — the priest laying the sacrifice in order (hinting the author was a priest, 'offering' the word to supply) — and 'look up' from the root of Mizpeh, a watch-tower, as the seer looks up in Hab. 2:1.
Gill takes 'in the morning' as confidence of a seasonable hearing and a resolve to seek God first of all, giving him the first of the day.

Spurgeon reads not a prayer but a resolution: David will not be dumb; morning is the fittest hour ('an hour in the morning is worth two in the evening'), prayer 'the key of the day and the lock of the night.'

debates.question: What is the figure behind 'I will direct my prayer'?

sides.position: an archer aiming his arrow at the mark and then looking up to see it strike
a priest arranging and preparing the pieces of the morning sacrifice on the altar

schools.summary: Henry sets the verse under 'a sin-hating God' — a warning that if we regard iniquity he will not hear (Ps. 66:18), and an encouragement against wicked enemies; Spurgeon turns it into the plea, praying against 'the very things which thou thyself abhorrest.'
Clarke renders 'the evil man shall not even sojourn with thee'; Wesley: God does not approve of or delight in the wicked or their prayers, nor have any fellowship with them.
Ellicott renders 'the wicked man is not thy guest,' pointing to God's dwelling with the contrite (Isa. 57:15) and the acceptable worshipper of Ps. 15.
Gill: sin is the abominable thing God's righteous soul hates, yet his hatred of the sin is not inconsistent with his delight in the persons of his elect in Christ.

themes: God takes no pleasure in wickedness

schools.summary: Gill takes 'the foolish' morally — the proud self-praisers, boasters elated with their own excellency (Syriac 'the proud,' Chaldee 'mockers'); 'shall not stand' denotes God's abhorrence and denial of favour.
Clarke: the wicked man is a fool and madman fighting the Almighty; on 'thou hatest all workers of iniquity' he marvels at their portion, 'the hatred of God Almighty.'
Ellicott renders 'foolish' literally as 'shiners' — displayers of self, boasters — and glosses 'shall not stand' by men standing before kings (Prov. 22:29) and angels in the heavenly court (Job 1:6).
Henry: sin is folly and sinners the greatest fools, not of God's making but of their own; wicked people hate God, and justly are hated of him to their ruin.

themes: God hates all workers of iniquity
no standing before a holy God

schools.summary: Gill takes 'leasing' as a lie, doctrinal or common; God destroys liars by disease (Gehazi), sudden death (Ananias and Sapphira), or everlasting destruction, for all liars have their part in the lake of fire.
Clarke traces 'leasing' to the Anglo-Saxon for falsity, and reads 'the bloody man' as 'the man of bloods,' for a murderer's spirit rarely ends with one bloodshedding.
Ellicott notes 'bloody' is literally 'of bloods and deceit,' as the ancient versions render, joining violence and treachery in the one man.

Henry marks two sorts of sinner — the false, hateful to the God of truth, and the cruel, hateful to the God of mercy — liars and murderers resembling the devil, the very characters of David's enemies.

themes: the God of truth and the God of mercy
liars and murderers as the devil's children

schools.summary: Henry: God's holiness invites rather than terrifies the upright, who worships publicly ('the closet prepares us for, not excuses us from, public ordinances') and reverently 'in thy fear' (Heb. 12:28); Spurgeon turns the eyes spiritually to the heavenly temple — 'we open our hearts towards heaven.'

Clarke: it is 'in the multitude of thy mercy,' not merit, that David approaches, prostrate in self-abasement, taking 'temple' of the holy of holies or the heavenly temple in Christ; Wesley glosses holy boldness, trust only in mercy, holy dread.

Ellicott insists 'house … temple' be taken literally, not spiritually (against Hupfeld), the titles not framed with historical exactness; Keil and Delitzsch: David has access 'by the greatness and fulness of divine favour' to the tabernacle on Zion where the ark stood.
Gill fixes the 'house' as the tabernacle of Moses (the temple not yet built), which David, in a kind of exile, was confident to enter again.

debates.question: How can David worship 'toward thy holy temple' when only the tabernacle yet stood?

sides.position: take 'house … temple' literally of the sanctuary; the psalm-titles were not framed with historical exactness
'temple' means the holy of holies within the tabernacle, or the heavenly temple where God is met in Christ
David turned his eyes spiritually to the temple of God's holiness in heaven

themes: I will come into thy house

schools.summary: Gill weighs 'thy righteousness' as God's imputed righteousness, or his righteous statutes, or his leading 'for his righteousness' sake' — for the way of man is not in himself.
Ellicott fixes 'enemies' as 'those watching for' or lying in wait (Aquila and Jerome, 'those lying in ambush'); to walk in God's way is to walk in safety.

Henry: the watchers' malice made David more cautious, that they 'find no occasion against him' (answered in 1 Sam. 18:14); Spurgeon: led as a child by its father or a blind man by his friend, learning to give up our own way.

Clarke: we need God not only to bring us to his house but 'to keep our feet while we are there,' and to make his way straight before us; Wesley glosses 'the way' as the way God would have him walk, 'plain' to discern and follow.

Ellicott reads 'wickedness' as 'an abyss' (root 'to fall'), an introverted parallelism with 'mouth' answering 'tongue,' and 'flatter' as 'make smooth the tongue' (Ps. 12:2, cf. Milton's dissembling fiend).

Clarke reads the throat 'gaping for the dead,' effluvia destructive to the living, a picture of the whole human race; Wesley: the throat 'wide opened, ready to devour,' a metaphor from wild beasts gaping for prey.

Henry: the throat 'an open sepulchre, cruel as the grave' that never says 'enough' (Prov. 30:15-16), quoted in Rom. 3:13 for the corruption of mankind; Spurgeon presses Paul's use of it for 'all men by nature,' with the comfort of a resurrection of characters.
Gill: no steadfastness, nothing sure or firm in their mouth; true of Christ's enemies and of false teachers who handle the word deceitfully — 'an assembly of treacherous men.'

Ellicott renders 'destroy' literally 'make or count guilty,' 'transgressions' as 'revolts,' and notes the LXX/Vulgate 'let their plots fail'; Keil and Delitzsch dwell on the verb uniting guilt, the feeling of guilt, and expiation, and on God called Elohim here 'as being God the Judge.'

Henry: cast them out of the heritage and land of the living, fallen 'by their own counsels' (Ps. 7:15), his prayer 'from a spirit of prophecy, not of revenge,' resting on 'they have rebelled against thee'; Spurgeon: 'against thee, not against me,' the psalmist speaking as a judge ex officio, God's mouth.
Gill reads 'destroy thou them' as a prayer, weighing 'make them guilty' — that they appear guilty to themselves or be condemned — and destroyed soul and body.
Clarke would translate the imprecatory verbs in the future tense as prophetic: 'Thou wilt destroy them; thou wilt cast them out.'

debates.question: Are the words 'destroy thou them' an imprecation (petition) or a prophecy (declaration)?

sides.position: a petition asking God to make the enemies guilty and destroy them
a prophecy to be read in the future tense — 'Thou wilt destroy them'
both a prayer and a spirit of prophecy, grounded on their rebellion against God

schools.summary: Henry unfolds the fulness of the joy — 'joyful in thee … not in any creature,' defended as by the pillar of cloud and fire — and draws a rule of intercession, to pray for all who trust God and love his name; Spurgeon: joy is the believer's privilege, weeping now but rejoicing eternally, God the well-spring of bliss.
Gill: the glad ones trust not in themselves but in the name, righteousness, and strength of the Lord, rejoicing in his salvation and the hope of eternal glory.
Clarke again reads the words declaratively and prophetically: 'all those who put their trust in thee shall rejoice, shall ever shout for joy.'
Ellicott notes 'rejoice' from a root whose primary sense is 'bright,' echoing 'the light of the righteous rejoiceth' (Prov. 13:9).

themes: praying for all who love God's name

schools.summary: Henry: the righteous trust God and love his name; a shield guards one side, but God's favour is a defence on every side, like the hedge about Job (Job 1:10); Spurgeon hears in the encircling shield both glory and guard, the people 'heirs of blessedness,' crowned as with a royal helmet (Ainsworth).
Gill unfolds the blessing — imputed righteousness, forgiveness, all spiritual blessings, grace here and glory hereafter — whence the righteous have just reason to rejoice.
Ellicott names the shield tsinnah, the long large shield fit for a giant (1 Sam. 17:7) that covers the whole body, recalling Luther's 'under the shield of heaven.'

Clarke reads 'with favour' as 'like a shield, thy favour will crown him,' God's love their defence in all times, bidding us 'keep yourselves in the love of God' (Jude 21) — the morning's devotion 'a model by which every Christian may frame his own.'

themes: compassed with favour as a shield
